text: Smoke, song and the smell of spilled drink fill the common room. Sellswords trade rumours by the fire, a notice board sags under old contracts, and the keeper keeps the good barrels behind the bar.
A low roof, a smoky fire and a keeper who counts every coin twice. The ale is thin, the stew is mostly turnip, and nobody asks where your sword has been.
Rain drums on the shutters while a lone fiddler saws at a tune nobody asked for. Two sellswords argue over a game of knucklebones in the corner.
The common room smells of wet dogs and old beer. A faded notice on the wall still promises a reward for a bandit who was hanged last spring.
The tavern has grown: a second hall for the sellswords, more beds upstairs and a busier notice board. Word of it travels with every caravan that stops here.
Every bench is taken. Caravan drivers swap road news with mercenary captains, and serving girls weave between them with trays of foaming tankards.
A travelling bard has the whole room on its feet, stamping along to a song about a battle half of them claim to have fought in.
Fresh rushes on the floor, a second hearth roaring, and a board crowded with Guild seals. Word of this place has spread.
The tavern is known far and wide. Famous companies drink in its halls, its board carries the richest contracts in the land, and its cellars hold brews found nowhere else.
Banners of famous companies hang from the rafters, each one paid for in blood. Lords drink here under false names, and the keeper pretends not to know them.
The cellars run deeper than the foundations of some keeps, and tonight the keeper is pouring from a barrel older than the Empire.
Guild agents, foreign envoys and the costliest killers in the land share one long table, and somehow nobody has drawn steel. Yet.
A portrait of the Emperor hangs crooked over the hearth, and the sausages are as heavy as the opinions.
A knight in muddy armour is loudly composing a poem about his own valour, and the peasants are pretending to listen.
The vodka is poured by the bottle, the stove never goes out, and a bear sleeps by the door like a guard dog.
Every tankard bears a clan rune, the ale is strong enough to strip rust, and the keeper keeps a grudge-ledger behind the bar.
The furniture has been rebuilt more times than the walls, mostly from other furniture.
The wine is very red, the windows are very shuttered, and the staff never seem to blink.
Elegant cups of pale wine are served with quiet disdain, and the harpist plays as if the guests are not there.
The drinks are excellent, the knives are hidden, and every guest is careful to watch the others' hands.
Roots grow through the floor, lanterns glow in the branches overhead, and the cider was pressed by hands older than the trees.
The air is thick and warm, the drinks are served in carved gourds, and a skink tallies every coin on a stone tablet.
Everything is sticky, the ale glows faintly green, and something is always scratching inside the walls.
The bar is a sarcophagus, the keeper has been dead for some centuries, and the dust in the beer is older than the Empire.
Fishing nets hang from the ceiling, the grog is mostly salt, and the band is made of drowned sailors who will not stop playing.
Mead flows from horns as long as an arm, and every argument is settled by headbutt.
The herd drinks from troughs, the music is drums and bellowing, and the guests are judged by how loudly they roar.
The tables are scarred by blades, the patrons wear their Dark Gods' marks proudly, and the keeper counts skulls as well as coin.
Brawls are the entertainment, the floor is sand to soak the blood, and the keeper pours only for those who win.
The stew is green, the flies are friendly, and everyone is in far better spirits than they have any right to be.
Silk drapes, sweet smoke and music that never quite ends. Guests come for one drink and wake three days later.
The drinks change colour as they are poured, the stairs lead somewhere new each night, and the keeper answers questions before they are asked.
Fine tea is served alongside rice wine, lanterns line the eaves, and a scholar is copying the gossip down for the Celestial Court.
The portions are enormous, the chairs are reinforced, and the keeper weighs every guest on the way in to set the price.
The beer is brewed beside a forge, slaves carry the kegs, and the keeper's hat is taller than the doorway.
Tonight a hooded stranger in the corner has bought the whole room a round, and nobody knows why.
Tonight a wrestling match between two sellswords has spilled out into the yard, and the wagers are flying.
Tonight the keeper is in a foul mood: someone has drunk the good barrel dry.
Tonight a caravan has just come in from the road, its drivers full of news of armies on the move.
Tonight a wedding party has taken over the long table, and the whole tavern is invited.
Tonight a Guild inspector sits by the door, writing in a little book and frowning at the prices.
Tonight an old veteran is telling the tale of a battle for the third time, and it has grown bigger every time.
Tonight the roof leaks over the best table, so the most dangerous man in the room is sitting in a puddle and daring anyone to laugh.
